title: Push Pull Legs Upper Lower 5 days split Program review
summary: Reviews a viewer's 5-day PPL + upper/lower program (low volume, strength + hypertrophy balance, busy life). He widens the narrow 5-6 rep ranges or replaces them with a top set plus 3x5 backoff, scraps the pec deck, swaps pulldowns for pull-ups, adds deadlifts, merges redundant face pulls/reverse flies, moves the upper day to Wednesday, and merges leg and lower days into one big pre-weekend lower session with supersets and giant sets to raise density and save time.

claims.claim: A 5-6 rep range is too narrow to act as an evolving rep range: one rep of room doesn't let you manipulate volume and intensity; widen it.
A 5-6 rep range is still better than a fixed 3x5 or 5x5.
If you don't want to push volume and struggle to balance intensity and life, you'll eventually still have to push one of the two to get more tonnage.
For bench and overhead press, do a top set in the 2-4 rep range to push intensity, then a 3x5 as lower-intensity sandbagged volume, separating intensity and volume qualities.
Scrap the pec deck: it's just squeezing, can create shoulder pain and is a fairly unnatural joint motion you never do in real life.
Replace pec deck squeezing with push-ups or standing elastic band flies supersetted between bench and OHP sets; crossing across the clavicle hits upper and inner chest better.
Overhead cable extensions are a machine French press, great for the triceps long head, which is critical after bench/OHP already worked the medial and lateral heads.
Superset overhead cable extensions with lateral raises (3x10-12); they complement bench and OHP well.
Deadlifts let you pile up a lot of lower-body tonnage early in a session with heavy loads, saving time on other lower-body movements.
He is 'not Mr Intensity': he pushes tonnage with volume, doing higher-rep heavy squats and deadlifts that never go near 100%, which are safe, don't wreck him for a week, and save time.
Rows should be done in higher rep ranges because the upper back needs volume; low-rep rows break form and stop targeting the upper back.
If you do low-rep rows, Pendlay rows and dead-stop cheat rows are the best options.
3 sets of 5-6 won't drive progress past the novice stage; 3x5/5x5 should be used as extra lower-intensity volume. For a main row, use an evolving range of 4-7/8 or 4-6 reps.
Pendlay rows focus more on upper back (rear delts, traps); Yates rows focus more on mid back and lats, so they complement each other.
Supinated Yates rows are dangerous for the biceps; he advises against them.
Do pull-ups instead of lat pulldowns; if you can pulldown a lot but can't match the reps with bodyweight pull-ups, there's an imbalance.
Pull-ups are better even purely for hypertrophy because of the lat stretch and spinal decompression.
He doesn't hate machines: if you like the feel of a machine, use it.

Supersetting face pulls with reverse flies is pointless because both hit traps and rear delts; good supersets pre-fatigue a helper muscle so the target is unassisted. Pick one, apply both lifts' volume to it, and rotate them.
3 sets of 8-10 curls is not enough biceps volume even with a second curl session in the week.

Start the pull day by warming up to one peak deadlift set of 2-5 reps, then higher-rep Pendlay rows supersetted with pull-ups (use straps if grip limits), drop Yates rows, finish with 6x10-12 reverse flies and 6x8-10 curls.
A narrow range like 10-12 across 6 sets implies sandbagging (12 on the first set and 10 on the last), which is fine when the focus is volume rather than pushing progression.
Two workouts with the same tonnage, one done in 2 hours and one in 4, differ in intensity: the denser one is more intense, a way to raise intensity without hurting your life.
When adding deadlifts and these changes, start light and see how it affects recovery.
Don't follow a pull day with legs: rows fatigue the lower back and hamstrings. Do the upper day next; upper body recovers faster and 48 hours is enough.
Incline bench is fine if you like it for upper chest; use a top set plus 3x5 or a wider evolving range rather than 3x5-6.
Adding dumbbell work on the accessory upper day helps avoid overuse injuries, but decline pressing is dangerous for the shoulders.
Two days after the push day, keep the accessory upper day at lower volume (3x8-10).

Giant sets of movements working different muscles (rows, curls, face pulls) don't hurt strength but push cardiovascular endurance into the red, add metabolic fatigue, replace cardio and raise intensity, saving time.
Squats (knee flexion) are more taxing than deadlifts due to more actual loading; people think deadlifts are most taxing because poor form overloads the lower back instead of hamstrings and glutes.
Merge leg and lower days into one longer session on Thursday or Friday, giving three full days of recovery over the weekend before the deadlift day and one free day to schedule.
Use 3 sets of 4-6 on squats instead of 3x5 to have room to add weight.

Front squats after back squats work well: for most people the front squat is limited by thoracic extension and front rack, not legs, so pre-fatiguing the legs equalizes them and works the legs harder.
A 3x5 on front squats after squats is fine as extra tonnage, not as the progression lift.
Superset RDLs (3x8) with leg press (3x10), and front squats with pull-ups to finish off the upper back since it gets three days to recover.
Doing calisthenics like pull-ups even when not fully recovered improves recovery and doesn't hurt muscle building.
Finish the lower day with 3 rounds of a non-stop giant set: leg extensions 10, leg curls 10, calf raises 12, abs 15.
45 calf reps per week is low; add calves on another day (e.g. push day), since which day you train calves doesn't matter.
Final structure: four training days, with the heaviest, highest-tonnage day right before the weekend so it gets the most recovery time.

exercises.why: better upper and inner chest squeeze than pec deck; superset between presses

exercises.why: long head of triceps after pressing

exercises.why: lots of lower-body tonnage quickly, saves time

cues: use straps if supersetting with pull-ups

exercises.why: mid back and lats; supinated is risky for biceps

exercises.why: same muscles; supersetting them is redundant
